pos: n. (proper name; a head of Ephraim who stood against bringing Judah's captives into Samaria)
etymology: Hebrew Yechizqiyahu, the LORD strengthens, from chazaq, to be strong, with the divine name — the same name as Hezekiah.
biblical_def: Jehizkiah is one of four heads of Ephraim who did a thing almost without parallel in the history of the northern kingdom: they stopped their own victorious army and made it release its prisoners. “Then certain of the heads of the children of Ephraim, Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, and Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and Amasa the son of Hadlai, stood up against them that came from the war” (2 Chronicles 28:12). Their argument was not about politics but about guilt: “And said unto them, Ye shall not bring in the captives hither: for whereas we have offended against the LORD already, ye intend to add more to our sins and to our trespass: for our trespass is great, and there is fierce wrath against Israel” (2 Chronicles 28:13). The army obeyed: “So the armed men left the captives and the spoil before the princes and all the congregation” (2 Chronicles 28:14). And then these men did what the New Testament would later put in a parable: “And the men which were expressed by name rose up, and took the captives, and with the spoil clothed all that were naked among them, and arrayed them, and shod them, and gave them to eat and to drink, and anointed them, and carried all the feeble of them upon asses, and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brethren: then they returned to Samaria” (2 Chronicles 28:15).

corruption_summary: Mercy to an enemy is thought a modern discovery; four princes of apostate Israel clothed, fed and carried home the captives of Judah.
corruption_paragraphs: The good Samaritan is treated as an innovation of the gospel, and some suppose the Old Testament knows nothing of such a thing. Second Chronicles twenty-eight has four men of the northern kingdom clothe the naked, shoe them, feed them, anoint them, set the feeble on asses and bring them home — to captives of the rival kingdom, taken in a war their own side had won. Our Lord's parable was not without precedent in His own Scriptures.

What drove them was the fear of adding sin to sin. They did not say the prisoners deserved better; they said the trespass of Israel was already great and the wrath of God already fierce. A sound doctrine of guilt made them merciful, which is the opposite of what is usually alleged against it.

pos: n. (proper name; a descendant of Sheshan in the line of Jerahmeel)
etymology: Hebrew Yeqamyah, the LORD raises up or may the LORD establish, from qum, to rise or stand, with the divine name.
biblical_def: Jekamiah belongs to the line of Jerahmeel, in the genealogy of Judah: “And Eleasah begat Sisamai, and Sisamai begat Shallum” (1 Chronicles 2:40), and then “And Shallum begat Jekamiah, and Jekamiah begat Elishama” (1 Chronicles 2:41). The chapter turns at once to another branch: “Now the sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel were, Mesha his firstborn, which was the father of Ziph; and the sons of Mareshah the father of Hebron” (1 Chronicles 2:42). He must be carefully distinguished from another man of nearly the same name, a son of Jeconiah in the royal house: “Malchiram also, and Pedaiah, and Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah” (1 Chronicles 3:18). The Authorized Version spells the two differently — Jekamiah of Jerahmeel's line, Jecamiah of the captive king's — and they are two men in two different houses, four centuries apart. Jekamiah's name says the LORD raises up, and nothing is told of him but his father and his son; the raising up was the line itself, carried through men whose only recorded act was to beget the next.

corruption_summary: Similar names are collapsed into one man; Jekamiah of Jerahmeel's line and Jecamiah of the royal house are two, and the AV spells them apart.
corruption_paragraphs: Careless reading merges men whose names are close, and careless criticism then charges Scripture with the confusion. The Authorized Version keeps Jekamiah and Jecamiah distinct in spelling, and the two stand in different genealogies separated by centuries — one in the house of Jerahmeel, one among the sons of the captive Jeconiah. Attention to the text resolves what haste turns into an error.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God raises up a line by men who do nothing the history records, and that careful reading of the registers honours the God who gave them.

pos: n. (proper name; the father of Zechariah, one of Isaiah's faithful witnesses)
etymology: Hebrew Yeberekyahu, the LORD blesses or whom the LORD blesses, from barak, to bless, with the divine name.
biblical_def: Jeberechiah is named once, as the father of one of the two men Isaiah called to witness a prophecy before it came to pass. The LORD commanded the prophet to write a name in public: “Moreover the LORD said unto me, Take thee a great roll, and write in it with a man's pen concerning Mahershalalhashbaz” (Isaiah 8:1). Then the witnesses: “And I took unto me faithful witnesses to record, Uriah the priest, and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah” (Isaiah 8:2). Only afterwards was the child born who would bear the name: “And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son. Then said the LORD to me, Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz” (Isaiah 8:3), and the prophecy was dated by the child's infancy: “For before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria” (Isaiah 8:4). The whole procedure is a public, attested, dated prediction, witnessed by two named men before the event. Jeberechiah's only distinction in Scripture is that he raised a son whom a prophet would call a faithful witness.

corruption_summary: Prophecy is said to be written after the event; Isaiah wrote this one on a great roll, before witnesses, before the child was conceived.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard account of biblical prophecy is that it was composed after the fact and dated backwards. Isaiah eight was designed to make that impossible. The LORD told the prophet to write the name on a great roll with a man's pen — in plain, public lettering — and to take two named men as witnesses to the record, and only then was the child born whose infancy would measure the fulfilment.

The two witnesses were real and public men, one of them a priest. The prophecy was deposited, attested and dated in advance, and then Damascus and Samaria fell within the term. This is not a text that asks to be believed on sentiment.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Judah whose four sons are named in the Chronicles)
etymology: Hebrew Yehalel'el, he shall praise God, from halal, to praise, and 'el, God; named once, at 1 Chronicles 4:16.
biblical_def: Jehaleleel is a man of Judah, named once, with his four sons: “And the sons of Jehaleleel; Ziph, and Ziphah, Tiria, and Asareel” (1 Chronicles 4:16). The surrounding verses are a patchwork of Judah's houses and trades: “And Meonothai begat Ophrah: and Seraiah begat Joab, the father of the valley of Charashim; for they were craftsmen” (1 Chronicles 4:14); “And the sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh; Iru, Elah, and Naam: and the sons of Elah, even Kenaz” (1 Chronicles 4:15); and “And the sons of Ezra were, Jether, and Mered, and Epher, and Jalon: and she bare Miriam, and Shammai, and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa” (1 Chronicles 4:17). His name is a whole sentence of worship: he shall praise God. It is the same root that gives us hallelujah. A father in Judah gave his son a name that was a vow, and the son in turn named a son Ziph and another Ziphah, and the family went down into the registers with nothing recorded of them but that they existed and what they were called.

corruption_paragraphs: A name today is a matter of taste, and parents choose by sound. Hebrew parents regularly made a name into a declaration or a prayer, and this one is a clause: he shall praise God, built on the root that gives the church its hallelujah. Every time the child was called, a confession was spoken over him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the speech of a godly household, down to the names it gives its children, should be shaped by the praise of God.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Zerubbabel)
etymology: Hebrew Yushab-chesed, mercy shall be returned or lovingkindness is restored, from shub, to return, and chesed, mercy or lovingkindness.
biblical_def: Jushab-hesed is a son of Zerubbabel, the governor who led the first return from Babylon and laid the foundation of the second temple. The line is given thus: “And the sons of Pedaiah were, Zerubbabel, and Shimei: and the sons of Zerubbabel; Meshullam, and Hananiah, and Shelomith their sister” (1 Chronicles 3:19), and then “And Hashubah, and Ohel, and Berechiah, and Hasadiah, Jushabhesed, five” (1 Chronicles 3:20). The royal line is traced on past him: “And the sons of Hananiah; Pelatiah, and Jesaiah: the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shechaniah” (1 Chronicles 3:21), down to the last generation the Chronicler knew: “And the sons of Elioenai were, Hodaiah, and Eliashib, and Pelaiah, and Akkub, and Johanan, and Dalaiah, and Anani, seven” (1 Chronicles 3:24). The name is a confession of the whole return: mercy shall be returned. A man whose grandfather had been carried to Babylon named his son for the restoring of God's lovingkindness, and his brother Hasadiah — the LORD is kind — bears a name from the same root.

corruption_summary: Restoration is read as a national recovery; Zerubbabel named a son mercy shall be returned and meant God's lovingkindness.
corruption_paragraphs: The return from Babylon can be told as a political event: a decree, a caravan, a rebuilt wall. The man who led it named one son the LORD is kind and another mercy shall be returned. He did not reckon the restoration a matter of Persian policy. He reckoned it the coming back of the chesed of God to a people who had forfeited it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every recovery of God's people is a return of His undeserved mercy, and that the royal line of promise ran on through the sons of a governor with no throne.

pos: n. (proper name; a Merarite Levite, father of Ethan the singer, also called Kishi)
etymology: Hebrew Qushayahu, perhaps the bow of the LORD; the margin of the Authorized Version at 1 Chronicles 6:44 notes that Kishi there is the same name.
biblical_def: Kushaiah is the father of Ethan, one of the three chief singers David appointed when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem. The commission is given first: “And David spake to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brethren to be the singers with instruments of musick, psalteries and harps and cymbals, sounding, by lifting up the voice with joy” (1 Chronicles 15:16). Then the three men: “So the Levites appointed Heman the son of Joel; and of his brethren, Asaph the son of Berechiah; and of the sons of Merari their brethren, Ethan the son of Kushaiah” (1 Chronicles 15:17). Their instrument is specified: “So the singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were appointed to sound with cymbals of brass” (1 Chronicles 15:19). And the man set over the singing is named with the reason for his appointment: “And Chenaniah, chief of the Levites, was for song: he instructed about the song, because he was skilful” (1 Chronicles 15:22). Three families, three men, and a trained master of the music. Kushaiah's name is in Scripture because his son led one third of the worship of Israel.

corruption_summary: Skill in worship is suspected as professionalism; David appointed a chief for the song because the man was skilful.
corruption_paragraphs: Zeal and competence are set against each other, so that a trained musician in the church is thought to be a step toward performance. The account of the ark's coming up to Jerusalem says plainly that Chenaniah was made chief for the song because he was skilful, and that three Levitical families were appointed to the work with named instruments. Order and skill were part of the obedience.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is to be praised with trained skill and appointed order, by men set apart to it, and with the voice lifted up in joy.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Shemaiah, of the house of Obed-edom, a porter of the temple)
etymology: Hebrew Semakyahu, the LORD has sustained or the LORD upholds, from samak, to lean upon or support, with the divine name.
biblical_def: Semachiah is a grandson of Obed-edom, numbered among the Levitical porters of the house of the LORD. His father's house is introduced with a commendation: “Also unto Shemaiah his son were sons born, that ruled throughout the house of their father: for they were mighty men of valour” (1 Chronicles 26:6), and then the brothers are named: “The sons of Shemaiah; Othni, and Rephael, and Obed, Elzabad, whose brethren were strong men, Elihu, and Semachiah” (1 Chronicles 26:7). The house is counted: “All these of the sons of Obededom: they and their sons and their brethren, able men for strength for the service, were threescore and two of Obededom” (1 Chronicles 26:8), and the next house after: “And Meshelemiah had sons and brethren, strong men, eighteen” (1 Chronicles 26:9). Obed-edom was the man in whose house the ark had rested three months, and whom the LORD blessed for it. Sixty-two of his descendants served at the doors of the temple, called able men for strength for the service. A single act of reverent hospitality toward the ark of God left a house of doorkeepers two generations later.

pos: n. (proper name; the overseer of the singers at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Yizrachyah, the LORD will shine forth or the LORD arises, from zarach, to rise or shine; named once, at Nehemiah 12:42.
biblical_def: Jezrahiah is the overseer of the singers on the day the wall of Jerusalem was dedicated. The preparation is described: “And at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem they sought the Levites out of all their places, to bring them to Jerusalem, to keep the dedication with gladness, both with thanksgivings, and with singing, with cymbals, psalteries, and with harps” (Nehemiah 12:27). Two companies went round the wall in opposite directions, with trumpets: “And the priests; Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets” (Nehemiah 12:41), and then the singers, with their overseer: “And Maaseiah, and Shemaiah, and Eleazar, and Uzzi, and Jehohanan, and Malchijah, and Elam, and Ezer. And the singers sang loud, with Jezrahiah their overseer” (Nehemiah 12:42). And the day is summed up: “Also that day they offered great sacrifices, and rejoiced: for God had made them rejoice with great joy: the wives also and the children rejoiced: so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off” (Nehemiah 12:43). The singers sang loud, the wives and children rejoiced, and the sound carried out of the city — and the man who had charge of that singing is named.

corruption_summary: Loud, public joy in worship is thought unseemly; at the dedication of the wall God made His people rejoice so that it was heard afar off.
corruption_paragraphs: Restraint is now treated as the mark of serious worship, and audible gladness as a lapse of taste. The dedication of Jerusalem's wall was neither restrained nor accidental: the Levites were fetched out of all their places for it, the singers sang loud under an appointed overseer, and the text says that God had made them rejoice with great joy. The joy was His work and it was heard out of the city.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God gives His people joy, that He appoints men to lead their singing, and that the wives and children belong in the congregation's rejoicing.

pos: n. (proper name; a priest of the house of Sallai in the days of Joiakim)
etymology: Hebrew Qallay, perhaps swift or light, from qal, swift; named once, at Nehemiah 12:20.
biblical_def: Kallai is a priest named in the register of the heads of the priestly houses in the days of Joiakim the son of Jeshua. The list runs in pairs, the house and its head: “And of Joiarib, Mattenai; of Jedaiah, Uzzi” (Nehemiah 12:19); “Of Sallai, Kallai; of Amok, Eber” (Nehemiah 12:20); “Of Hilkiah, Hashabiah; of Jedaiah, Nethaneel” (Nehemiah 12:21). Then the Chronicler of this book states what the register is for: “The Levites in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, and Johanan, and Jaddua, were recorded chief of the fathers: also the priests, to the reign of Darius the Persian” (Nehemiah 12:22). The priesthood of Israel depended on descent; a man who could not prove his line could not serve at the altar. So the names were kept, generation by generation, under Persian rule, in a city still half-ruined, by men who understood that a lost register meant a lost ministry. Kallai is a name in that keeping.

corruption_summary: Records are thought a dead formality; in Israel a priest without a register could not serve, so the names were kept under foreign rule.
corruption_paragraphs: It is easy to treat the keeping of records as bureaucracy and the lists in Nehemiah as the residue of it. For a priest in Israel the register was his ministry. Those who came up from Babylon and could not find their genealogy were put from the priesthood until a decision could be had, and so the houses were recorded, head by head, down to the reign of Darius the Persian.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appointed His ministry by His own order and not by willingness, and that faithful record-keeping is a service to the generations that follow.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Shemaiah, of the house of Obed-edom, a porter of the temple)
etymology: Hebrew Repha'el, God has healed, from rapha, to heal, and 'el, God; named once, at 1 Chronicles 26:7.
biblical_def: Rephael is a grandson of Obed-edom and one of the Levitical porters of the house of the LORD: “The sons of Shemaiah; Othni, and Rephael, and Obed, Elzabad, whose brethren were strong men, Elihu, and Semachiah” (1 Chronicles 26:7). His father's house is commended in the verse before: “Also unto Shemaiah his son were sons born, that ruled throughout the house of their father: for they were mighty men of valour” (1 Chronicles 26:6). The whole family is then numbered: “All these of the sons of Obededom: they and their sons and their brethren, able men for strength for the service, were threescore and two of Obededom” (1 Chronicles 26:8), and the next house follows: “And Meshelemiah had sons and brethren, strong men, eighteen” (1 Chronicles 26:9). His name means God has healed. It is the same Hebrew root that stands behind the name by which God revealed Himself to Israel at the waters of Marah, and behind the promise that by His stripes we are healed. A Levite at a temple gate carried that confession as his name, and the Spirit of God wrote it down.

corruption_summary: Healing is claimed as a right to be demanded; a Levite's name confesses it as something God has already done.
corruption_paragraphs: Healing is widely presented as a benefit the believer may require of God on demand, and faith measured by whether he gets it. The name Rephael is in the perfect tense: God has healed. It is a confession of a thing received, from the same root as the name God took to Himself at Marah, and it was borne by a man who stood at a gate for a living.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is the healer of His people in His own time and way, and that the deepest healing He promises is by the stripes of His Son.
